summary: Toki Sherbakov and Anoop Kotha from OpenAI's solution architecture team present patterns and best practices for building production voice agents. The talk situates audio within the broader multimodal AI evolution—text-first applications expanding to images, video, and now high-quality speech-to-speech. Audio models have crossed a usability tipping point: previously slow, robotic, and brittle, they are now fast, expressive, and accurate enough for production-scale applications. A demo contrasts an older voice model with a current one to illustrate this shift. Two architectures are presented: the chained approach (transcription, LLM, TTS as three separate models—functional but slow and lossy) and speech-to-speech via OpenAI's real-time API (single model, reducing latency and preserving context). Five trade-offs shape architecture decisions: latency, cost, accuracy/intelligence, user experience, and integrations. Consumer apps prioritize UX and latency; customer service apps prioritize accuracy and integrations. Anoop defines an agent as model plus instructions plus runtime, noting voice agents require distinct attention to system design, voice customization, tools, and evaluation. Delegation through tools is a key pattern: the real-time API serves as frontline agent, delegating harder tasks to smarter models like o4-mini. Voice prompting extends beyond instructions to control expressiveness, tone, and enthusiasm, with few-shot examples mirroring text-based prompting for complex conversation flows. Tool use should start simple—limited tools per agent—with handoffs managing context via conversation summarization to avoid lossy transfers. Evaluation breaks into four buckets: observability (traces of agent behavior), human-labeled data for prompt iteration, transcription-based evals (LLM-as-judge, function-calling rubrics), and audio or synthetic conversation evals (using models like GPT-4 Audio for tone and pacing, or simulating multi-agent conversations). Guardrails should run asynchronously since generated text outpaces spoken audio, with configurable debounce periods. Customer learnings include Lemonade's early focus on evals and guardrails, and Tinder's emphasis on customization and brand realism. Toki concludes that a new real-time API snapshot makes this the moment to build production voice applications.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Multimodal AI Context
sections.summary: Toki introduces himself and Anoop from OpenAI's solution architecture team. He situates audio within the evolution from text-based GenAI to multimodal era (images, video, audio), noting that speech-to-speech low latency experiences are reaching a production tipping point where models are fast, expressive, and accurate.

sections.title: Voice Model Demo: Old vs New
sections.summary: A side-by-side demo contrasts older voice models (slow, robotic, brittle—failed to follow interruption, wrote about sand instead of stars) with current models (fast, expressive, accurate—successfully changed topic from whispers to stars with emotional delivery). Illustrates the tipping point in audio model quality.

sections.title: Audio Agent Architectures
sections.summary: Two architectures are presented: the chained approach (audio in, transcription, LLM intelligence layer, TTS out—three models stitched together, slow and lossy) and the speech-to-speech architecture (single model via real-time API handling all layers, reducing latency and preserving semantic understanding).

sections.title: Trade-offs by Use Case
sections.summary: Five trade-offs (latency, cost, accuracy/intelligence, user experience, integrations/tooling) vary by use case. Consumer-facing apps prioritize UX and latency; customer service apps prioritize accuracy (wrong order numbers are unacceptable) and integrations with internal systems, SIP, and phone providers.

sections.title: Agent Definition and Voice-Specific Considerations
sections.summary: Anoop defines an agent as model + instructions (prompts, tools) + runtime (guardrails, execution environment). Voice agents require distinct attention to system design, prompting and voice customization, tools, and eval/guardrails compared to traditional text-based agents.

sections.title: Delegation Pattern and Voice Prompting
sections.summary: Covers the delegation-through-tools pattern where real-time API serves as frontline agent, delegating harder tasks to smarter models like o4-mini via tool calls (demoed in a retail return scenario). Also introduces voice prompting capabilities for controlling expressiveness, demeanor, tone, and enthusiasm beyond text instructions.

sections.title: Voice Prompting Playground and Few-Shot Examples
sections.summary: Introduces a website for experimenting with voice expressiveness and sample prompts, demonstrating the performance ceiling and fluctuation achievable through prompting alone. Extends voice prompting with few-shot examples mirroring text-based approaches—using greeting, description, and instruction structures for complex real-time API conversation flows.

sections.title: Tool Use, Handoffs, and Delegation
sections.summary: Covers tool use best practices for voice agents: start simple with limited tools per agent, add more as needed. Handoffs between agents require context preservation via conversation state summarization to avoid lossy transfers. Delegation via the agents SDK is natively supported for routing tasks to models like o3-mini or o4-mini.

sections.title: Evaluation Framework
sections.summary: Breaks voice agent evaluation into four buckets: observability (traces of agent behavior and audio), human-labeled data for prompt iteration (the most effective approach seen with customers), transcription-based evals (LLM-as-judge, function-calling rubrics), and audio or synthetic conversation evals (using models like GPT-4 Audio for tone, pacing, intonation, or simulating multi-agent conversations with customer personas).

sections.title: Guardrails and Customer Learnings
sections.summary: Guardrails for the real-time API should run asynchronously since generated text outpaces spoken audio, with configurable debounce periods (e.g., every 100 characters). Customer learnings: Lemonade (AI insurance) succeeded by focusing early on evals, guardrails, and feedback mechanisms even before scaling; Tinder prioritized customization and brand realism for their voice chat experience.

sections.title: Wrap-up and Call to Action
sections.summary: Toki wraps up by reiterating the multimodal era and announcing a new real-time API snapshot released the day before, described as significantly better. He encourages builders to take advantage of first-mover advantage now that the technology is production-ready.
